source: Cornell University Department of Plant Pathology and Plant-Microbe Biology / NYS IPM Ornamental Disease Guidelines
title: Maple Tar Spot (Rhytisma acerinum, teleomorph; anamorph Melasmia acerina) on Acer Species
content: Maple tar spot is the most conspicuous and easily recognized foliar disease of maple trees (Acer spp.) in North America and Europe. The causal organism is Rhytisma acerinum (Pers.) Fr. (phylum Ascomycota, class Leotiomycetes, order Rhytismatales, family Rhytismataceae); the asexual anamorphic stage is Melasmia acerina Lev. It is specific to the genus Acer and does not infect any other tree genera. The pathogen has been reported from all Acer-growing regions of the northeastern, midwestern, and northwestern United States, southern and eastern Canada, most of Europe (United Kingdom, Netherlands, Germany, France, Poland, Russia), western and central Asia, and northern Japan. Tar spot is primarily a cosmetic and aesthetic disease; it rarely causes significant long-term health damage to otherwise healthy, mature, well-established maple trees. However, severe, repeated consecutive annual infections (3+ years) on stressed or newly transplanted maple saplings and young nursery stock can cause 50-80% premature defoliation 2-4 weeks before normal autumn fall coloration, reduced annual diameter and height growth, reduced root system mass, increased susceptibility to secondary opportunistic canker fungi (Nectria, Botryosphaeria, Hypoxylon) and Armillaria root rot, and reduced overwintering cold-hardiness resulting in branch dieback. Two closely related species, R. punctatum (speckled tar spot of maples) and R. americanum (American tar spot of striped and mountain maple), produce morphologically similar symptoms but on different Acer host ranges. The most diagnostic symptom of maple tar spot is the development of tar-like, raised, shiny, jet-black, circular to slightly irregular lesions ('tar spots') on the upper (adaxial) surface of maple leaves, typically 5-25 mm in diameter, often with a narrow yellow chlorotic halo visible in early autumn before leaf senescence. The disease develops through three characteristic phases: (1) Phase 1 (early summer, mid-June through early July in the northeastern US): tiny, pale yellow-green, pinhead-sized speckled spots (0.5-2 mm) appear on newly fully expanded leaves; these early chlorotic lesions are often overlooked. (2) Phase 2 (mid-summer to late August): the yellow lesions expand and the central lesion portion develops into slightly sunken, brown, necrotic, speckled tissue containing asexual pycnidia of the Melasmia acerina anamorph, embedded in the host epidermal and palisade layers. (3) Phase 3 (early September through October, and continuing on overwintered fallen leaves in spring): the brown necrotic lesion centers rapidly enlarge and develop into the characteristic, raised, hard, brittle, shiny black stromatic fungal 'tar spots'. Each black tar spot is a thick (0.5-1 mm), sterile, carbonized, fungal stroma containing multiple embedded, flask-shaped, ostiolate spermogonia (early) and later multiple embedded apothecial locules of the Rhytisma acerinum teleomorph (mature in the following spring on fallen overwintered leaves). When tar spots are cut in cross-section and examined under a dissecting microscope, the characteristic layered structure of the stroma with embedded ascomata is visible. Heavily infected maple leaves may carry 5-50 tar spots per leaf blade. Severe infections occasionally cause partial or complete leaf blight when numerous lesions coalesce, but even in severe cases, the tree typically retains 50% or more of its functional green leaf canopy. Rhytisma acerinum overwinters on fallen infected maple leaves on the ground beneath or near the tree, where the thick black stromata survive the winter cold, snow cover, and spring rains. In spring, approximately at the time of Acer budbreak and new leaf emergence (April-May in the northeastern US), the apothecial locules embedded in the overwintered tar-spot stromata mature, and the stromatal upper surface cracks open in a stellate (star-shaped) pattern to expose the apothecial hymenium. Numerous club-shaped, bitunicate, 8-spored asci (120-160 x 10-14 um) forcibly discharge long, filiform, hyaline, septate ascospores (55-80 x 1.5-2 um) into the air during wet spring rain events. Ascospores are wind-dispersed 10-500 m from fallen leaves and are deposited onto the newly expanding, still-tender, lower-canopy maple leaves of the new growing season. Ascospores germinate through the young cuticle directly or via stomata, requiring 6-24 hours of continuous leaf wetness and temperatures of 12-20 C for successful infection; the infection court is closed once leaves are fully expanded and cuticular wax has hardened (usually by mid-June in temperate climates), which explains why only one primary infection cycle occurs per growing season. Secondary asexual inoculum (conidia from the Melasmia anamorph pycnidia in the mid-season brown lesions) is produced abundantly in July and August, splash-dispersed by rain, and is capable of causing scattered secondary spot infections under extended wet periods during years with particularly mild, wet July-August weather; however, in most years there is no significant secondary spread. R. acerinum host range within Acer: highly susceptible species include Norway maple (A. platanoides - the most susceptible, with tar spots up to 3 cm), silver maple (A. saccharinum), sycamore maple (A. pseudoplatanus, Europe), sugar maple (A. saccharum), red maple (A. rubrum, moderately susceptible); more resistant species include Japanese maple (A. palmatum, rarely infected in landscape), box elder (A. negundo, rare), striped maple (A. pensylvanicum, infected by R. americanum rather than R. acerinum), and mountain maple (A. spicatum). Management: (1) cultural practices are most effective and preferred for landscape, park, and shade-tree maple tar spot management, since the disease is primarily cosmetic: (a) collect, rake, remove, and destroy (municipal compost hot-processing, landfill, or burn) all fallen infected maple leaves from under and around affected trees in autumn BEFORE spring budbreak - this simple practice eliminates the entire local source of overwintering ascospores and reduces infection the following year by 80-95% if done consistently for 2 consecutive years. (b) avoid planting dense monoculture stands of highly susceptible Norway maple in close proximity to large, old sugar maple woodlots that serve as continuous tar spot inoculum reservoirs. (c) for high-value landscape and nursery trees, ensure adequate tree vigor through proper soil pH management (maples prefer pH 5.5-7.0), regular deep watering during summer drought, 5-10 cm of organic wood-chip mulch over the root zone, and a balanced N-P-K fertilization program to maintain photosynthetic capacity during partial defoliation years. (2) genetic resistance: among commonly planted landscape maples, Acer platanoides 'Crimson King', 'Emerald Queen', and 'Drummondii' are highly susceptible; A. rubrum 'Red Sunset', 'October Glory', and A. saccharum 'Legacy', 'Green Mountain' show moderate quantitative partial resistance. (3) fungicide sprays are rarely economically or aesthetically justified for most landscape trees, but may be applied to high-value nursery stock production or specimen Japanese maple or sugar maple in a sugar bush where tar spot has been > 50% defoliation for 2+ consecutive years. The most effective fungicide programs in Cornell and Penn State landscape IPM trials protect the newly emerging expanding leaves during the primary infection period (budbreak through full leaf expansion, approximately 3-5 sprays at 10-14 day intervals between early April and mid-June in the northeast). Effective materials: FRAC M3 multi-site protectant mancozeb (the gold standard for tar spot), FRAC M1 copper hydroxide / copper oxychloride (Bordeaux mixture acceptable in organic programs), FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (tebuconazole, propiconazole, myclobutanil, difenoconazole; good protectant + 2-3 day curative activity), FRAC 11 QoI (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin; good protectant), FRAC 7 SDHI (fluxapyroxad, penthiopyrad; protectant). All fungicides must be applied BEFORE spore deposition and infection; once yellow speckled Phase 1 spots are visible on leaves, no curative treatment will remove them. (4) biological control: experimental trials with foliar sprays of commercial formulations of the mycoparasitic fungi Ampelomyces quisqualis and Trichoderma atroviride, and of the yeast-like fungus Aureobasidium pullulans, have reduced tar spot incidence by 40-60% in European nursery trials, but these products are not currently registered for landscape maple tar spot control in the United States.
